concepts: One-one and onto functions via monotonicity of a cubic
questions.question: The function $f:[0,3]\to[1,29]$, defined by $f(x)=2x^3-15x^2+36x+1$, is:
questions.key_idea: A continuous function that rises and then falls on the interval cannot be one-one, and the endpoint and turning-point values give its range.
solution: On $[0,3]$: $f'>0$ for $x\in[0,2)$ and $f'<0$ for $x\in(2,3]$, so $f$ is non-monotonic on $[0,3]$.
Hence $f$ is increasing on $[0,2)$ and decreasing on $(2,3]$, so $f$ is not one-one.
The least value is $1$ and the greatest value is $29$, and $f$ is continuous, so the range of $f$ is $[1,29]$.
Range = codomain, so $f$ is onto.
$f$ is onto but not one-one: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Factor $f(x)-28$ and $29-f(x)$ to get an explicit repeated value and exact bounds, with no calculus.
solution: So $f\left(\frac32\right)=28=f(3)$ with $\frac32\neq3$: $f$ is not one-one.
$f(x)-1=x(2x^2-15x+36)$ and $2x^2-15x+36$ has discriminant $225-288<0$, so it is positive; hence $f(x)\ge1$ for $x\ge0$.
Thus $f([0,3])\subseteq[1,29]$, with $f(0)=1$ and $f(2)=29$ attained; $f$ is continuous, so by the intermediate value theorem every value of $[1,29]$ is taken.
So $f$ is onto but not one-one: (B).

useful_results: A continuous function on an interval is one-one iff it is strictly monotonic; a sign change of $f'$ inside the interval kills one-one-ness.
For a continuous $f$ on $[a,b]$, the range is $[\min,\max]$; the min and max are among $f(a),f(b)$ and the values at critical points.
For a cubic, $f(x)-f(c)$ always has the factor $(x-c)$; if $c$ is an endpoint at which $f'(c)\ne0$ the other factor is a quadratic, whose roots give repeated values.
Here $f(3/2)=f(3)=28$, a concrete pair showing the failure of one-one.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Finding a function from a functional relation with a substitution
Double-angle identities
questions.question: Let $f:(-1,1)\to\mathbb{R}$ be such that $f(\cos4\theta)=\frac{2}{2-\sec^2\theta}$ for $\theta\in\left(0,\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\cup\left(\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$. Then the value(s) of $f\left(\frac13\right)$ is (are):
questions.key_idea: Rewrite $\frac{2}{2-\sec^2\theta}$ in terms of $\cos2\theta$, then find which $\cos2\theta$ gives $\cos4\theta=\frac13$.
solution: $\theta\in\left(0,\frac\pi4\right)\cup\left(\frac\pi4,\frac\pi2\right)\Rightarrow 2\theta\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)\cup\left(\frac\pi2,\pi\right)$.
$f(\cos4\theta)=\frac{2}{2-\sec^2\theta}=\frac{2\cos^2\theta}{2\cos^2\theta-1}$, and $2\cos^2\theta=1+\cos2\theta$.
So $f(\cos4\theta)=\frac{1+\cos2\theta}{\cos2\theta}=1+\frac{1}{\cos2\theta}$ ......(i)
Let $\cos4\theta=\frac13$, i.e. $2\cos^22\theta-1=\frac13$.
Then $\cos^22\theta=\frac23$, so $\cos2\theta=\pm\sqrt{\frac23}$ (both signs are allowed because $2\theta$ can lie in $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$ or $\left(\frac\pi2,\pi\right)$).
From (i): $f\left(\frac13\right)=1\pm\sqrt{\frac32}$.
Hence options (A) and (B) are correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the half-angle form $\tan^22\theta=\frac{1-\cos4\theta}{1+\cos4\theta}$ so that only $\sec2\theta$ is needed.
solution: From (i), $f(\cos4\theta)=1+\sec2\theta$.
$\tan^22\theta=\frac{1-\cos4\theta}{1+\cos4\theta}$, and for $\cos4\theta=\frac13$ this is $\frac{2/3}{4/3}=\frac12$.
$\sec^22\theta=1+\tan^22\theta=\frac32$, so $\sec2\theta=\pm\sqrt{\frac32}$.
Therefore $f\left(\frac13\right)=1\pm\sqrt{\frac32}$, i.e. (A) and (B).

useful_results: $\frac{2}{2-\sec^2\theta}=\frac{2\cos^2\theta}{2\cos^2\theta-1}=\frac{1+\cos2\theta}{\cos2\theta}$: turn $\sec^2\theta$ into $\cos2\theta$ with $2\cos^2\theta=1+\cos2\theta$.
$\tan^2A=\frac{1-\cos2A}{1+\cos2A}$ and $\cos2A=2\cos^2A-1$ move between $\cos2A$ and $\sec A$ without solving for $A$.
When a function is defined through a parameter, the value at a point can have several branches; list every allowed branch of the parameter (here $\cos2\theta$ of either sign).
Remark: since $\cos2\theta=\pm\sqrt{2/3}$ give the same $\cos4\theta$ but different $f$, the relation does not define a single-valued $f$; the official key (A, B) takes both values.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Odd and even functions
One-one and onto functions
questions.question: Let $f:\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\to\mathbb{R}$ be given by $f(x)=\left(\log(\sec x+\tan x)\right)^3$. Then:
questions.key_idea: $\log(\sec x+\tan x)$ is odd, increasing and unbounded both ways, so its cube inherits all three properties.
solution: (i) $\sec x+\tan x=\frac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}$ and $\sec(-x)+\tan(-x)=\sec x-\tan x=\frac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}$.
So $f(-x)=\left(-\log(\sec x+\tan x)\right)^3=-f(x)$: $f$ is odd, so (A) is true and (D) is false.
(ii) $f'(x)=3\left(\log(\sec x+\tan x)\right)^2\cdot\frac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}\left(\sec x\tan x+\sec^2x\right)$.
Since $\sec x\tan x+\sec^2x=\sec x(\tan x+\sec x)$, $f'(x)=3\left(\log(\sec x+\tan x)\right)^2\sec x\ge0$, with equality only at $x=0$.
So $f$ is strictly increasing: one-one, (B) is true.
(iii) As $x\to-\frac\pi2^+$, $\sec x+\tan x\to0^+$ and $f(x)\to-\infty$; as $x\to\frac\pi2^-$, $f(x)\to+\infty$.
$f$ is continuous, so its range is $\mathbb{R}$: $f$ is onto, (C) is true.

alternate_solutions.idea: Recognise $\log(\sec x+\tan x)=\sinh^{-1}(\tan x)$, so $f$ is a composition of three odd increasing bijections.
solution: $\sec x+\tan x=\tan x+\sqrt{1+\tan^2x}$ (as $\sec x>0$ here), so $\log(\sec x+\tan x)=\sinh^{-1}(\tan x)$.
Hence $f(x)=\left(\sinh^{-1}(\tan x)\right)^3$, the composition $x\mapsto\tan x\mapsto\sinh^{-1}(\cdot)\mapsto(\cdot)^3$.
$\tan:\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)\to\mathbb{R}$, $\sinh^{-1}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ and the cube $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ are each odd, strictly increasing bijections.
A composition of odd functions is odd, and a composition of increasing bijections is an increasing bijection.
So $f$ is odd, one-one and onto: (A), (B), (C).

useful_results: $\log(\sec x+\tan x)=\sinh^{-1}(\tan x)=\int_0^x\sec t\,dt$ on $\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$: an odd, increasing bijection onto $\mathbb{R}$ (the inverse Gudermannian).
A composition of odd functions is odd; a composition of strictly increasing bijections is a strictly increasing bijection.
$\sec(-x)+\tan(-x)=\frac{1}{\sec x+\tan x}$ is the reason the log is odd; the same trick gives oddness of $\log\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)$.
A strictly increasing function can have $f'(x)=0$ at isolated points (here $x=0$), so check zeros of $f'$ before declaring it not one-one.

concepts: Counting one-one and onto functions
questions.question: Let $X$ be a set with exactly 5 elements and $Y$ be a set with exactly 7 elements. If $\alpha$ is the number of one-one functions from $X$ to $Y$ and $\beta$ is the number of onto functions from $Y$ to $X$, then the value of $\frac{1}{5!}(\beta-\alpha)$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Count onto maps $Y\to X$ by splitting the 7 elements into 5 non-empty groups (sizes $3,1,1,1,1$ or $2,2,1,1,1$) and sending the groups to $X$.
solution: One-one functions $X\to Y$: $\alpha={}^7C_5\times5!=21\times120=2520$.
Onto functions $Y\to X$: split the 7 elements of $Y$ into 5 non-empty groups (one group per element of $X$); the sizes are $3,1,1,1,1$ or $2,2,1,1,1$.
Sizes $3,1,1,1,1$: number of ways to form the groups $=\frac{7!}{3!\,4!}=35={}^7C_3$.
Sizes $2,2,1,1,1$: number of ways to form the groups $=\frac{7!}{2!\,2!\,2!\,3!}=105=3\cdot{}^7C_3$.
Assign the 5 groups to the 5 elements of $X$ in $5!$ ways: $\beta=(35+105)\times5!=4\cdot{}^7C_3\cdot5!=16800$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count onto maps $Y\to X$ by inclusion-exclusion on the missed elements of $X$, with no case analysis of group sizes.
solution: Number of maps $Y\to X$ missing a chosen set of $k$ elements of $X$ is $(5-k)^7$.
By inclusion-exclusion $\beta=\sum_{k=0}^{5}(-1)^k\,{}^5C_k(5-k)^7$.
$\alpha=7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3=2520$.

useful_results: Onto maps from an $m$-set to an $n$-set: $\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\,{}^nC_k(n-k)^m=n!\,S(m,n)$, where $S(m,n)$ is the Stirling number of the second kind.
The block sizes of an onto map $m\to n$ are the partitions of $m$ into exactly $n$ positive parts; for $7\to5$ they are only $3,1,1,1,1$ and $2,2,1,1,1$.
Number of ways to split $N$ labelled objects into groups of given sizes is $\frac{N!}{\prod(\text{size}!)\prod(\text{repeat count})!}$ when groups of equal size are unlabelled.

concepts: One-one and onto functions via monotonicity
questions.question: If the function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is defined by $f(x)=|x|(x-\sin x)$, then which of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.key_idea: $f$ is odd and increasing on $[0,\infty)$ because $x-\sin x\ge0$ and its derivative is non-negative, so it is increasing on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
solution: $f(x)=x(x-\sin x)$ for $x\ge0$ and $f(x)=-x(x-\sin x)$ for $x<0$.
For $x\ge0$: $f'(x)=2x-(\sin x+x\cos x)$.
$f'(x)=(x-\sin x)+x(1-\cos x)\ge0$, since $x\ge\sin x$ for $x\ge0$ and $\cos x\le1$.
So $f$ is increasing on $[0,\infty)$, and its least value there is $f(0)=0$.
As $x\to\infty$, $f(x)\to\infty$ ($f(x)\ge x(x-1)$); with continuity, $f([0,\infty))=[0,\infty)$.
For $x<0$: $f(-x)=|-x|(-x+\sin x)=-f(x)$, so $f$ is odd; hence $f$ is also increasing on $(-\infty,0)$ and $f\left((-\infty,0)\right)=(-\infty,0)$.
So the range of $f$ is $\mathbb{R}$: $f$ is onto.
$f$ is increasing on $\mathbb{R}$ (increasing on both sides, with $f(0)=0$ joining them), so $f$ is one-one.
$f$ is both one-one and onto: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $f(x)=x\cdot(x-\sin x)$ for $x\ge0$ as a product of two positive increasing functions, avoiding any derivative of the product.
solution: $f$ is odd: $f(-x)=|x|(-x+\sin x)=-f(x)$; it suffices to study $x\ge0$.
$u(x)=x-\sin x$ has $u'(x)=1-\cos x\ge0$, so $u$ is non-decreasing, $u(0)=0$, hence $u(x)>0$ for $x>0$ (strictly, since $\sin x<x$).
For $0<x_1<x_2$: $x_1<x_2$ and $0<u(x_1)\le u(x_2)$, so $x_1u(x_1)<x_2u(x_2)$: $f$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$, and $f(0)=0<f(x)$ for $x>0$.
By oddness, $f$ is strictly increasing on all of $\mathbb{R}$: one-one.
$f(x)\to\pm\infty$ as $x\to\pm\infty$ and $f$ is continuous, so the range is $\mathbb{R}$: onto. Answer (C).

useful_results: $\sin x<x$ for $x>0$, so $x-\sin x$ is positive and increasing on $(0,\infty)$; $x-\sin x$ is an odd, strictly increasing function on $\mathbb{R}$.
The product of two positive strictly increasing functions is strictly increasing; $|x|\cdot g(x)$ with $g$ odd is odd.
A continuous strictly increasing function $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f\to\pm\infty$ at $\pm\infty$ is a bijection; one-one plus these limits gives onto.
Same pattern: $x|x|$, $x^3+x$, $x+\sin x$, $|x|(x+\sin x)$ are all bijections of $\mathbb{R}$.

concepts: Symmetry property $f(x)+f(1-x)=$ constant and summation
questions.question: Let the function $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f(x)=\frac{4^x}{4^x+2}$. Then the value of $f\left(\frac{1}{40}\right)+f\left(\frac{2}{40}\right)+f\left(\frac{3}{40}\right)+\cdots+f\left(\frac{39}{40}\right)-f\left(\frac12\right)$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: $f(x)+f(1-x)=1$, so the terms $f\left(\frac{k}{40}\right)$ and $f\left(\frac{40-k}{40}\right)$ pair up to 1.
solution: $f(x)=\frac{4^x}{4^x+2}$; replace $x\to1-x$.
So $f\left(\frac1{40}\right)+f\left(\frac{39}{40}\right)=f\left(\frac{2}{40}\right)+f\left(\frac{38}{40}\right)=\cdots=f\left(\frac{19}{40}\right)+f\left(\frac{21}{40}\right)=1$.
The 39 terms are 19 such pairs plus the middle term $f\left(\frac{20}{40}\right)=f\left(\frac12\right)$.
The sum is $19+f\left(\frac{20}{40}\right)-f\left(\frac12\right)=19+f\left(\frac12\right)-f\left(\frac12\right)$.
The value is $19$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $f(x)-\frac12$ is an odd function of $x-\frac12$, so the deviations from $\frac12$ cancel in symmetric sums.
solution: Put $u=4^x/2=2^{2x-1}$: $f(x)-\frac12=\frac{u-1}{2(u+1)}$, which changes sign under $u\to\frac1u$, i.e. under $x\to1-x$.
So $h(x)=f(x)-\frac12$ satisfies $h(1-x)=-h(x)$ and $h\left(\frac12\right)=0$: the graph is symmetric about the point $\left(\frac12,\frac12\right)$.
$\sum_{k=1}^{39}h\left(\frac{k}{40}\right)=0$, since $k$ and $40-k$ cancel and the middle term $k=20$ is $0$.
$\sum_{k=1}^{39}f\left(\frac{k}{40}\right)=\frac{39}{2}$; subtract $f\left(\frac12\right)=\frac12$ to get $19$.

useful_results: For $f(x)=\frac{a^x}{a^x+c}$ with $c=\sqrt a$ (here $c=2=\sqrt4$): $f(x)+f(1-x)=1$. In general $\frac{a^x}{a^x+\sqrt a}$ has this property.
For $f(x)+f(1-x)=1$: $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}f\left(\frac kn\right)=\frac{n-1}{2}$ (with $f(1/2)$ the middle term when $n$ is even).
Recognition cue: a sum of $f(k/n)$ for $k=1..n-1$ always asks you to find $f(x)+f(c-x)$.
Check: $n=2$: $f\left(\frac12\right)=\frac12=\frac{2-1}{2}$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Range of a trigonometric function
Determinants of a skew-symmetric matrix
questions.question: Let $|M|$ denote the determinant of a square matrix $M$. Let $g:\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $g(\theta)=\sqrt{f(\theta)-1}+\sqrt{f\left(\frac\pi2-\theta\right)-1}$, where $f(\theta)=\frac12\left|\begin{matrix}1&\sin\theta&1\\-\sin\theta&1&\sin\theta\\-1&-\sin\theta&1\end{matrix}\right|+\left|\begin{matrix}\sin\pi&\cos\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)&\tan\left(\theta-\frac\pi4\right)\\\sin\left(\theta-\frac\pi4\right)&-\cos\frac\pi2&\log_e\frac4\pi\\\cot\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)&\log_e\frac\pi4&\tan\pi\end{matrix}\right|$. Let $p(x)$ be a quadratic polynomial whose roots are the maximum and minimum values of $g(\theta)$, and $p(2)=2-\sqrt2$. Then which of the following is/are TRUE?
questions.key_idea: The second determinant is skew-symmetric (so $0$), the first gives $f=1+\sin^2\theta$, hence $g=\sin\theta+\cos\theta\in[1,\sqrt2]$.
solution: Second determinant: simplify $\sin\pi=0$, $-\cos\frac\pi2=0$, $\tan\pi=0$; the entries below/above the diagonal are negatives of each other, e.g. $\sin\left(\theta-\frac\pi4\right)=-\cos\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)$ and $\cot\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)=-\tan\left(\theta-\frac\pi4\right)$.
So it is a $3\times3$ skew-symmetric determinant, and equals $0$.
First determinant: $1\left(1+\sin^2\theta\right)-\sin\theta(-\sin\theta+\sin\theta)+1\left(\sin^2\theta+1\right)=2\left(1+\sin^2\theta\right)$.
$f(\theta)=\frac12\cdot2\left(1+\sin^2\theta\right)+0=1+\sin^2\theta$.
$g(\theta)=\sqrt{\sin^2\theta}+\sqrt{\sin^2\left(\frac\pi2-\theta\right)}=|\sin\theta|+|\cos\theta|=\sin\theta+\cos\theta$ on $\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]$.
$g(\theta)\in\left[1,\sqrt2\right]$: minimum $1$ at $\theta=0,\frac\pi2$ and maximum $\sqrt2$ at $\theta=\frac\pi4$.
$p(x)=k(x-1)\left(x-\sqrt2\right)$ and $p(2)=k\left(2-\sqrt2\right)=2-\sqrt2$, so $k=1$: $p(x)=(x-1)\left(x-\sqrt2\right)$.
$p(x)<0$ exactly for $1<x<\sqrt2$ and $p(x)>0$ for $x<1$ or $x>\sqrt2$.
(A) $\frac{3+\sqrt2}{4}\approx1.10\in(1,\sqrt2)$: $p<0$, correct. (B) $\frac{1+3\sqrt2}{4}\approx1.31\in(1,\sqrt2)$: $p<0$, so '$>0$' is incorrect.
(C) $\frac{5\sqrt2-1}{4}\approx1.52>\sqrt2$: $p>0$, correct. (D) $\frac{5-\sqrt2}{4}\approx0.90<1$: $p>0$, so '$<0$' is incorrect.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\det M=\det M^T=\det(-M)=-\det M$ for a skew-symmetric $3\times3$ matrix, and $g=\sqrt2\sin\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)$ to read off the range.
solution: For the second matrix $B$ (odd order, $B^T=-B$): $\det B=\det B^T=\det(-B)=(-1)^3\det B$, so $\det B=0$.
Expanding the first determinant along row 1 gives $2(1+\sin^2\theta)$, so $f=1+\sin^2\theta$ and $g=\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\sqrt2\sin\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)$.
For $\theta\in\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]$, $\theta+\frac\pi4\in\left[\frac\pi4,\frac{3\pi}4\right]$ so $\sin(\cdot)\in\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt2},1\right]$ and $g\in[1,\sqrt2]$.
$p<0$ iff the argument lies strictly between the roots $1$ and $1.4142$. Decimal values of the four arguments: $1.1036,\ 1.3107,\ 1.5178,\ 0.8964$.
First two lie between the roots (so $p<0$): (A) true, (B) false. Last two lie outside (so $p>0$): (C) true, (D) false. Answer (A, C).

useful_results: A skew-symmetric matrix of odd order has determinant $0$ (because $\det A=\det A^T=\det(-A)=(-1)^n\det A$); look for this before expanding any determinant with $\pm$ mirrored entries and zero diagonal.
$a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta$ has range $\left[-\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\right]$; on $\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]$ the range of $\sin\theta+\cos\theta$ is $[1,\sqrt2]$.
For a monic quadratic with roots $\alpha<\beta$: $p(x)<0$ exactly on $(\alpha,\beta)$; compare each argument with the roots instead of evaluating $p$.
$\sqrt{u^2}=|u|$: always remove the root with the absolute value and then use the interval to decide the sign.

concepts: Zeros of $x^2\sin(\pi/x^2)$ and counting solutions in intervals
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function defined by $f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{x^2}\right),&\text{if }x\neq0\\0,&\text{if }x=0\end{cases}$. Then which of the following statements is TRUE?
options: $f(x)=0$ has infinitely many solutions in the interval $\left[\frac{1}{10^{10}},\infty\right)$
$f(x)=0$ has no solutions in the interval $\left[\frac1\pi,\infty\right)$
The set of solutions of $f(x)=0$ in the interval $\left(0,\frac{1}{10^{10}}\right)$ is finite
$f(x)=0$ has more than 25 solutions in the interval $\left(\frac{1}{\pi^2},\frac1\pi\right)$
questions.key_idea: For $x>0$, $f(x)=0\iff x=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}$ with $n$ a positive integer, so counting solutions in an interval is counting integers $n$.
solution: For $x>0$: $f(x)=0\Rightarrow x^2\sin\left(\frac\pi{x^2}\right)=0\Rightarrow\sin\left(\frac\pi{x^2}\right)=0$.
So $\frac\pi{x^2}=n\pi$ with $n$ a positive integer, i.e. $x=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}$, $n=1,2,3,\dots$ (negative $x$ and $x=0$ are outside all the intervals).
(A) $x\ge\frac{1}{10^{10}}\iff\frac1{\sqrt n}\ge10^{-10}\iff n\le10^{20}$: only finitely many solutions, so (A) is false.
(B) $x\ge\frac1\pi\iff\frac1{\sqrt n}\ge\frac1\pi\iff n\le\pi^2\approx9.87$: the solutions $n=1,\dots,9$ exist, so (B) is false.
(C) $0<x<\frac1{10^{10}}\iff n>10^{20}$: infinitely many solutions, so (C) is false.
(D) $x\in\left(\frac1{\pi^2},\frac1\pi\right)\Rightarrow\frac1{\pi^2}<\frac1{\sqrt n}<\frac1\pi\Rightarrow\pi<\sqrt n<\pi^2$.
Squaring, $\pi^2<n<\pi^4$, i.e. $9.87<n<97.41$: the integers $n=10,11,\dots,97$, which is $88$ values.
$88>25$, so $f(x)=0$ has more than 25 solutions there: (D) is true.
questions.correction_note: The PDF checks only option (D) and its last lines are cut (it ends at n>=2, 2<=n<=4). Options (A), (B), (C) were added and the count in (D) was completed: pi^2 < n < pi^4 gives n = 10..97, i.e. 88 solutions. The answer (D) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use a counting function: the number of zeros that are $\ge c$ is $\left\lfloor\frac{1}{c^2}\right\rfloor$, so zeros in an interval are a difference of two floors.
solution: Positive zeros are $x_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}$, decreasing in $n$; the number of zeros $x\ge c$ is $N(c)=\left\lfloor c^{-2}\right\rfloor$.
(A) $N(10^{-10})=10^{20}$ is finite, (B) $N(1/\pi)=\lfloor\pi^2\rfloor=9\ne0$, so false.
(C) Zeros in $\left(0,10^{-10}\right)$ are those with $n>10^{20}$: unbounded, infinitely many, so false.
(D) Zeros in $\left(\frac1{\pi^2},\frac1\pi\right)$ number $N\left(\frac1{\pi^2}\right)-N\left(\frac1\pi\right)$ (neither endpoint is a zero) $=\lfloor\pi^4\rfloor-\lfloor\pi^2\rfloor=97-9=88>25$.
Only (D) is true.

useful_results: $x^2\sin\left(\frac\pi{x^2}\right)$ oscillates infinitely often near $0$: zeros $x_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}$ accumulate only at $0$, so any interval $[c,\infty)$, $c>0$, has finitely many zeros and every $(0,c)$ has infinitely many.
For $\sin\left(\frac{k}{x^m}\right)$-type functions, zeros satisfy $\frac{k}{x^m}=n\pi$; convert 'zeros in an interval' to 'integers $n$ in an interval' and count with floors.
Number of integers in the open interval $(a,b)$ is $\lceil b\rceil-\lfloor a\rfloor-1$; here $\pi^2\approx9.87$, $\pi^4\approx97.41$.
Useful decimals: $\pi^2\approx9.8696$, $\pi^3\approx31.006$, $\pi^4\approx97.409$.

concepts: Additive and multiplicative functional equations
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function such that $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$, and $g:\mathbb{R}\to(0,\infty)$ be a function such that $g(x+y)=g(x)g(y)$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$. If $f\left(-\frac35\right)=12$ and $g\left(-\frac13\right)=2$, then the value of $\left(f\left(\frac14\right)+g(-2)-8\right)g(0)$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Additive gives $f(qx)=qf(x)$ and multiplicative gives $g(nx)=g(x)^n$ for rational multiples, enough to reach $\frac14$ and $-2$.
solution: $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ for all $x,y$, so $f(x)=ax$; $f\left(-\frac35\right)=12$ gives $a=-20$.
So $f(x)=-20x$ and $f\left(\frac14\right)=-5$.
$g(x+y)=g(x)g(y)$ for all $x,y$, so $g(x)=k^x$; $g\left(-\frac13\right)=2$ gives $2=k^{-1/3}$.
So $k=\left(2^{-1}\right)^3=\frac18$ and $g(x)=\left(\frac18\right)^x$.
$\left(f\left(\frac14\right)+g(-2)-8\right)g(0)=(-5+64-8)\cdot1=51$.
questions.correction_note: Not a wrong answer. The PDF assumes f(x)=ax and g(x)=k^x, which the question does not justify (no continuity is given; non-linear additive functions exist). Wording kept, but the step is now justified as in the alternate: only rational multiples of the given points are needed, so f(qx)=q f(x) and g(qx)=g(x)^q. The answer 51 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use only rational homogeneity, $f(qx)=qf(x)$ and $g(nx)=g(x)^n$, so no continuity or formula for $f,g$ is assumed.
solution: From $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$: $f(nx)=nf(x)$ for integers $n$ and hence $f(qx)=qf(x)$ for every rational $q$.
$\frac14=\left(-\frac{5}{12}\right)\left(-\frac35\right)$ with $-\frac5{12}$ rational, so $f\left(\frac14\right)=-\frac5{12}\cdot12=-5$.
From $g(x+y)=g(x)g(y)$: $g(nx)=g(x)^n$ for integer $n$, and $g(0)=g(0)^2$ with $g>0$ gives $g(0)=1$.
$-2=6\cdot\left(-\frac13\right)$, so $g(-2)=g\left(-\frac13\right)^6=2^6=64$.
$\left(-5+64-8\right)\cdot1=51$.

useful_results: Cauchy additive equation: $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$ forces $f(qx)=qf(x)$ for all rational $q$, and $f(0)=0$; $f(x)=ax$ for all real $x$ needs extra regularity (continuity, monotonicity, boundedness).
Exponential equation: $g(x+y)=g(x)g(y)$ with $g>0$ gives $g(0)=1$, $g(-x)=\frac1{g(x)}$ and $g(qx)=g(x)^q$ for rational $q$.
When the asked points are rational multiples of the given points, rational homogeneity suffices and the answer does not depend on regularity.
Here $f(x)=-20x$ and $g(x)=8^{-x}$ satisfy the data; check: $f(-3/5)=12$, $g(-1/3)=8^{1/3}=2$.

concepts: Counting relations on a finite set
questions.paragraph: Let $S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ and $X$ be the set of all relations $R$ from $S$ to $S$ that satisfy both the following properties: (i) $R$ has exactly 6 elements. (ii) For each $(a,b)\in R$, we have $|a-b|\ge2$. Let $Y=\{R\in X:\text{the range of }R\text{ has exactly one element}\}$ and $Z=\{R\in X:R\text{ is a function from }S\text{ to }S\}$. Let $n(A)$ denote the number of elements in a set $A$.
questions.question: If $n(X)={}^mC_6$, then the value of $m$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: A relation is a subset of the allowed ordered pairs, so $n(X)=\binom{N}{6}$ where $N$ is the number of pairs with $|a-b|\ge2$.
solution: A relation $R$ with property (ii) is a subset of $T=\{(a,b)\in S\times S:|a-b|\ge2\}$, and property (i) says it has exactly 6 elements; so $n(X)={}^{n(T)}C_6$.
Counting row by row: $4+3+3+3+3+4=20$ pairs.
Check by complement: $36-\left(6\text{ pairs with }a=b\right)-\left(10\text{ pairs with }|a-b|=1\right)=20$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Classify the allowed pairs by the difference $d=|a-b|$: for each $d$ there are $2(6-d)$ ordered pairs.
solution: For a fixed $d\ge1$ the unordered pairs $\{a,a+d\}$ with $1\le a\le6-d$ number $6-d$, each giving 2 ordered pairs, so $2(6-d)$ ordered pairs.
$d=2,3,4,5$ give $8,6,4,2$ ordered pairs.

useful_results: A relation from $A$ to $B$ is a subset of $A\times B$; the number of relations satisfying a condition on each pair is $2^{N}$ ($N$ = allowed pairs), and with exactly $r$ pairs it is $\binom Nr$.
Number of ordered pairs in $\{1..n\}^2$ with $|a-b|=d$ is $2(n-d)$ for $1\le d\le n-1$; total with $|a-b|\ge2$ is $(n-1)(n-2)$.
Check: $(6-1)(6-2)=20$ matches.

concepts: Counting relations and functions on a finite set
questions.paragraph: Let $S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ and $X$ be the set of all relations $R$ from $S$ to $S$ that satisfy both the following properties: (i) $R$ has exactly 6 elements. (ii) For each $(a,b)\in R$, we have $|a-b|\ge2$. Let $Y=\{R\in X:\text{the range of }R\text{ has exactly one element}\}$ and $Z=\{R\in X:R\text{ is a function from }S\text{ to }S\}$. Let $n(A)$ denote the number of elements in a set $A$.
questions.question: If the value of $n(Y)+n(Z)$ is $k^2$, then $|k|$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: A relation in $Z$ is a function with 6 pairs: pick one allowed image for each $a$; one in $Y$ would need 6 pairs with one common second element, which is impossible.
solution: $Y$: all 6 pairs must have the same second element $b$, so $b$ must be allowed with 6 different first elements; but any $b$ is allowed with at most 4 first elements.
Hence $n(Y)=0$.
$Z$: a function $S\to S$ has exactly 6 pairs $(a,f(a))$, one for each $a$, so property (i) is automatic; property (ii) needs $f(a)$ in the allowed set of $a$.
$n(Z)=4\times3\times3\times3\times3\times4=1296$.
useful_results: A function $S	o S$ with an allowed set $A_a$ for each input $a$ is counted by the rule of product $\prod|A_a|$; here $|A_a|=4,3,3,3,3,4$.
If a restriction allows each output value for at most $m$ inputs, no function with a single repeated value on more than $m$ inputs exists (pigeonhole), which is why $n(Y)=0$.
A relation with exactly $n$ pairs on an $n$-set is a function only if every input appears once; so $Z$ is the set of relations whose first components are $1,\dots,6$ each once.

concepts: Polynomial functions with no real solution of $f(x)=g(x)$
questions.question: Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the set of all real numbers. Let $a_i,b_i\in\mathbb{R}$ for $i\in\{1,2,3\}$. Define the functions $f,g,h:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by $f(x)=a_1+10x+a_2x^2+a_3x^3+x^4$, $g(x)=b_1+3x+b_2x^2+b_3x^3+x^4$, $h(x)=f(x+1)-g(x+2)$. If $f(x)\neq g(x)$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$, then the coefficient of $x^3$ in $h(x)$ is:
questions.key_idea: $f(x)-g(x)$ has degree at most 3 and no real root, so its cubic coefficient must vanish: $a_3=b_3$.
solution: $f(x)\neq g(x)$ for every real $x$ means the equation $f(x)=g(x)$ has no real solution.
A polynomial of odd degree always has a real root, so the cubic term must be absent: $a_3=b_3$.
Then the quadratic $(a_2-b_2)x^2+7x+(a_1-b_1)$ has no real root, which needs $49-4(a_2-b_2)(a_1-b_1)<0$ (this is a condition on the other constants, not needed for the coefficient).
The $x^3$ terms: from $a_3(x+1)^3$: $a_3$; from $b_3(x+2)^3$: $b_3$; they cancel as $a_3=b_3$. The squares and linear terms have no $x^3$.
On the right only $(x+1)^4-(x+2)^4$ contributes: $x^3$ coefficient is ${}^4C_1\cdot1-{}^4C_1\cdot2=4-8=-4$.
So the coefficient of $x^3$ in $h(x)$ is $-4$: option (C).
useful_results: A real polynomial of odd degree takes all real values, so $P(x)=0$ always has a real root; 'no real root' forces the leading term of the difference to be of even degree.
Coefficient of $x^{n-1}$ in $(x+c)^n$ is $nc$: here $4\cdot1-4\cdot2=-4$ without expanding.
For $f(x)=x^n+\cdots$, $f(x+s)$ has $x^{n-1}$ coefficient $a_{n-1}+ns$; the shift changes only the next-to-leading coefficient by $ns$.
Check with $f=x^4$, $g=x^4+1$ (so $f\neq g$ everywhere): $h=(x+1)^4-(x+2)^4-1$ has $x^3$ coefficient $4-8=-4$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Composition of functions
One-one and onto functions on $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$
questions.question: Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the set of all natural numbers, and $\mathbb{Z}$ denote the set of all integers. Consider the functions $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$ and $g:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{N}$ defined by $f(n)=\begin{cases}\frac{n+1}{2},&n\text{ odd}\\\frac{4-n}{2},&n\text{ even}\end{cases}$ and $g(n)=\begin{cases}3+2n,&n\ge0\\-2n,&n<0\end{cases}$. Define $(g\circ f)(n)=g(f(n))$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and $(f\circ g)(n)=f(g(n))$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: $g\circ f$ is NOT one-one and $g\circ f$ is NOT onto
$f\circ g$ is NOT one-one but $f\circ g$ is onto
$f$ is NOT one-one but $f$ is onto
questions.key_idea: Tabulate $f$, $g$ and the compositions: $f$ repeats the value 1, while $g$ never takes the value 1, and $f\circ g(n)=n+2$ is a bijection.
solution: $f(1)=f(2)=1$, so $f$ is not one-one; odd $n$ give $1,2,3,\dots$ and even $n$ give $1,0,-1,-2,\dots$, so every integer is a value: $f$ is onto. (D) is true.

$g$ takes the odd values $3,5,7,\dots$ and the even values $2,4,6,\dots$, each once: $g$ is one-one, but it never takes the value $1$, so $g$ is not onto. (C) is false (the PDF's statement that $g$ is not one-one is incorrect).
$(f\circ g)(n)$: for $n\ge0$, $g(n)=3+2n$ is odd, so $f(g(n))=\frac{4+2n}{2}=n+2$; for $n<0$, $g(n)=-2n$ is even, so $f(g(n))=\frac{4+2n}{2}=n+2$.
So $(f\circ g)(n)=n+2$ for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, which is one-one and onto: (B) says 'not one-one', so (B) is false.
$(g\circ f)(n)$ for $n=1,\dots,8$: $5,5,7,3,9,2,11,4$; since $f(1)=f(2)$, $g\circ f(1)=g\circ f(2)=5$: $g\circ f$ is not one-one.
The range of $g\circ f$ is contained in the range of $g$, which misses $1$: $g\circ f$ is not onto. So (A) is true.
Hence the correct options are (A) and (D).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's tables (f, f(g), g(f)) and the final answer (A, D) are right, but it states that g is 'not one-one and into'. g is one-one (g(0)=3, g(1)=5, ... odd values; g(-1)=2, g(-2)=4, ... even values, no value repeats); it is only not onto (1 is missed). Corrected the statement; (C) is still false, the answer is unchanged. Also the paper prints the definition of g with the letter f; read as g.

alternate_solutions.idea: General theorem: $f\circ g$ injective $\Rightarrow g$ injective; $f\circ g$ surjective $\Rightarrow f$ surjective. Then $f\circ g(n)=n+2$ settles everything quickly.
solution: Compute $f\circ g(n)=n+2$ for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ (odd and even branches both give $n+2$): a bijection of $\mathbb{Z}$.
$f\circ g$ one-one $\Rightarrow g$ is one-one; $f\circ g$ onto $\Rightarrow f$ is onto. So $f$ is onto and $g$ is one-one.
$f$ is not one-one since $f(1)=f(2)=1$: (D) true. $g$ misses $1$ (values are $\ge2$), so $g$ is not onto: (C) false; and (B) is false because $f\circ g$ is one-one.
$g\circ f$: as $f(1)=f(2)$, $g\circ f$ is not one-one; its range is within $g(\mathbb{Z})\not\ni1$, so it is not onto: (A) true.
Answer (A, D).

useful_results: $g\circ f$ injective $\Rightarrow f$ injective; $g\circ f$ surjective $\Rightarrow g$ surjective. Conversely, if $f$ is not injective then $g\circ f$ is not injective; if $g$ is not onto then $g\circ f$ is not onto.
A quick test for a piecewise function with an odd/even or sign split: list its first 8-10 values, spot repeated values (not one-one) and missing values (not onto), then prove the pattern.
Interlacing pattern: positive integers from one branch and non-positive integers from another make a bijection with $\mathbb{Z}$ (here $f$ is $2\to1$ at value 1, otherwise a bijection).
$f(g(n))=n+2$ shows $g$ is a one-sided inverse of a shift: $g$ is a right inverse of $f$ up to translation.

concepts: Multiplicative functional equation and arithmetic-geometric sequences
questions.question: Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the set of all real numbers. Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function such that $f(x)>0$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$, and $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$. Let the real numbers $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_{50}$ be in an arithmetic progression. If $f(a_{31})=64f(a_{25})$, and $\sum_{i=1}^{50}f(a_i)=3\left(2^{25}+1\right)$, then the value of $\sum_{i=6}^{30}f(a_i)$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: $f(a_i)$ is a geometric progression with ratio $f(D)$; the condition $f(a_{31})=64f(a_{25})$ gives ratio $\sqrt[6]{64}=2$.
solution: $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$ with $f>0$: take $f(x)=a^x$ ($a>0$); the terms $f(a_i)=a^{A+(i-1)D}$ form a geometric progression.
Let the AP have first term $A$ and common difference $D$: $a_{31}=A+30D$, $a_{25}=A+24D$.
$f(a_{31})=64f(a_{25})\Rightarrow a^{A}a^{30D}=64\,a^{A}a^{24D}\Rightarrow\left(a^{D}\right)^6=64$.
Since $a^D>0$, $a^D=2$ (the PDF takes $a=2$, $D=1$, but only the ratio $r=a^D=2$ matters).
$\sum_{i=6}^{30}f(a_i)=a^{A+5D}\left(1+r+\cdots+r^{24}\right)=a^A\cdot2^5\cdot\left(2^{25}-1\right)$.
questions.correction_note: The answer 96 is correct. The PDF writes '6 a^(6D) = 2^6 => a=2; D=1' and then uses a=2, D=1; that is not forced (a^(6D)=64 only gives the ratio a^D=2). Replaced by the ratio r=a^D=2, which is all the later steps use; the final computation is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split the 50 terms into two blocks of 25: the second block is $2^{25}$ times the first, so each block sum is found without solving for the first term.
solution: $b_i=f(a_i)$ is a GP with ratio $r$; $b_{31}=64b_{25}$ gives $r^6=64$, so $r=2$.

useful_results: If $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)$ and $f>0$, then $f$ of an AP is a GP with ratio $f(D)$: this turns sums over an AP into geometric sums.
Shifting the window of a GP sum multiplies it by a power of the ratio: $\sum_{i=m+1}^{m+n}b_i=r^m\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i$.
$\sum_{i=1}^{2n}b_i=\left(1+r^n\right)\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_i$: halving a GP sum when the whole sum has a factor $1+r^n$.
Check numerically: with $r=2$, $b_1=\frac{3}{2^{25}-1}$ the full sum is $b_1(2^{50}-1)=3(2^{25}+1)$ and the sum from $6$ to $30$ is $96$.

concepts: Equivalence relations and partitions of a set
questions.question: Let $S=\{1,2,3,\dots,10\}$. Consider the set $X=\{R:R\text{ is an equivalence relation on the set }S\text{ such that }R\text{ has exactly 42 elements}\}$. Then the number of elements in $X$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: An equivalence relation is a partition into classes, and a class of size $x$ contributes $x^2$ ordered pairs; solve $\sum x_i=10$, $\sum x_i^2=42$.
solution: $R$ has exactly 42 ordered pairs. Reflexivity forces all 10 pairs $(a,a)$ to be in $R$, leaving $42-10=32$ other pairs.
Symmetry makes the other pairs come in twin pairs $(a,b),(b,a)$ with $a\neq b$: $\frac{32}{2}=16$ such pairs.
Transitivity with symmetry means elements related to each other form closed groups (equivalence classes) in which every element is related to every element of the same group.
A class with $x$ elements contributes exactly $x^2$ ordered pairs. If the classes have sizes $x_1,\dots,x_k$: $x_1+\cdots+x_k=10$ and $x_1^2+\cdots+x_k^2=42$.
The solutions are: Case I: sizes $6,2,1,1$ ($36+4+1+1=42$); Case II: sizes $5,4,1$ ($25+16+1=42$).
Number of ways to split $n$ distinct objects into classes of sizes $p,q,r,\dots$ is $\frac{n!}{(p!\,q!\,r!\cdots)\,a!\,b!\cdots}$ where $a,b,\dots$ are the repeat counts of equal sizes.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count unordered related pairs instead: $\sum\binom{x_i}{2}=16$, which also gives a quick way to see why only two partitions work, then count by choosing classes with binomials.
solution: The number of unordered related pairs $\{a,b\}$, $a\ne b$, is $\sum\binom{x_i}{2}=\frac{42-10}{2}=16$ with $\sum x_i=10$.
$\binom x2$ for $x=1,\dots,7$ is $0,1,3,6,10,15,21$; a class of size $7$ or more gives at least $21>16$, so every class has size $\le6$.

Write $16$ as a sum of these values with total size $10$: $15+1$ (classes of size $6$ and $2$, plus two singletons) and $10+6$ (classes of size $5$ and $4$, plus one singleton); any other split, e.g. $10+3+3$ or $6+6+3+1$, needs more than $10$ elements.
Sizes $\{6,2,1,1\}$: choose the 6-class $\binom{10}{6}=210$, then the 2-class from the remaining 4: $\binom42=6$; the last two are singletons: $210\times6=1260$.
Sizes $\{5,4,1\}$: choose the 5-class $\binom{10}5=252$, then the 4-class from the remaining 5: $\binom54=5$: $252\times5=1260$.

useful_results: Equivalence relations on an $n$-set $\leftrightarrow$ partitions of the set; a relation with classes of sizes $x_i$ has $\sum x_i^2$ ordered pairs and $\sum x_i=n$.
Equivalent form: number of unordered related pairs is $\sum\binom{x_i}{2}$; for a fixed number of elements, larger classes give more pairs ($\sum x_i^2$ is convex).
Number of ways to partition $n$ labelled objects into classes with sizes $p_1,\dots$: $\frac{n!}{\prod p_i!\prod m_j!}$ ($m_j$ = number of classes of the same size $j$).
Bell numbers count all equivalence relations on an $n$-set ($B_{10}=115975$); here only the partitions with $\sum x^2=42$ are counted.

concepts: Counting one-one functions with restrictions
Composition of functions: left inverse exists iff one-one
questions.question: Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the set of all positive integers. Consider the sets $A=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ and $B=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}$. Let $S$ be the set of all functions $f:A\to B$ such that $f(2)\neq2$ and $f(4)\neq4$. Consider the set $T=\{f\in S:\text{there exists a function }g:B\to\mathbb{N}\text{ such that }g(f(x))=2x\text{ for all }x\in A\}$. Then the number of elements in the set $T$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: A $g$ with $g(f(x))=2x$ exists iff $f$ is one-one, so count one-one maps $A\to B$ with $f(2)\ne2$, $f(4)\ne4$ by inclusion-exclusion.
solution: $g(f(x))=2x$ for all $x\in A$: since $x\mapsto2x$ is one-one, $f$ must be one-one (if $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ then $2x_1=2x_2$).
Conversely, if $f$ is one-one, define $g(f(x))=2x$ on $f(A)$ and arbitrarily elsewhere; so $T$ is the set of one-one $f$ with $f(2)\neq2$, $f(4)\ne4$.
Total one-one functions $A\to B$: $7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3=2520$.
With $f(2)=2$: the other 4 elements map one-one into the remaining 6 values: ${}^6C_4\cdot4!=360$; similarly with $f(4)=4$: $360$.
With $f(2)=2$ and $f(4)=4$: the other 3 elements map one-one into the remaining 5 values: ${}^5C_3\cdot3!=60$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count directly: first choose the images of the restricted positions 2 and 4, then fill the other three positions, with no complement.
solution: $f$ must be one-one; choose $f(2)\neq2$ first: $6$ choices.

Choose $f(4)
e4$ and $f(4)
eq f(2)$: if $f(2)=4$ (1 case) then $f(4)$ has $6$ choices (any value except $4$); if $f(2)
otin\{2,4\}$ (5 cases) then $f(4)\in B\setminus\{4,f(2)\}$ has $5$ choices.
Number of ordered choices of $(f(2),f(4))$: $1\cdot6+5\cdot5=31$.
The positions $1,3,5$ take distinct values from the remaining $5$ elements of $B$: $5\cdot4\cdot3=60$.
Total $=31\times60=1860$.

useful_results: A function $f:A\to B$ has a 'left inverse' $g$ with $g(f(x))=h(x)$ for a given $h$ iff $f(x_1)=f(x_2)\Rightarrow h(x_1)=h(x_2)$; if $h$ is one-one this means $f$ is one-one.
Counting injections with forbidden fixed points $f(i)\neq i$: inclusion-exclusion, $|\text{all}|-\sum|f(i)=i|+\sum|f(i)=i\text{ and }f(j)=j|-\cdots$.
Number of one-one maps from a $k$-set to an $n$-set: $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$; fixing $j$ points leaves $(n-j)(n-j-1)\cdots$ for the rest.
